reading.rtitle: Opening an Office in the US? The Bribery Rules Are Coming With You
paras: When a Brazilian company opens an office in the United States, its lawyers usually worry about taxes, employment contracts and corporate structure. Rarely do they think first about bribery. Yet not only does American anti-bribery law apply to the new American company; in some situations it can also reach the parent company in Brazil and the people who work for it. This is what lawyers call the extraterritorial reach of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the FCPA, a federal law that has been in force since 1977.

The central rule is simple. A company may not offer anything of value to a foreign official in order to win or keep business. Anything of value means exactly that: not only cash, but also a lavish dinner, a trip, or a job for an official's relative. Nor can a company hide behind an intermediary. If an agent or a consultant pays a bribe on the company's behalf, and the company knew about it or chose to turn a blind eye, the company is responsible. Companies whose shares trade in the US must also keep accurate books and records, so a bribe disguised as a consulting fee becomes a second problem.

Hospitality itself is not a crime. A reasonable business dinner with a client is normal in every country. Only when a gift is meant to buy a decision, as part of a quid pro quo, does it become a bribe; but the more lavish the dinner, the harder that is to explain. The real gray area is the facilitation payment. The FCPA allows a narrow exception for small payments that only speed up a routine action, such as processing a permit. Brazil's Clean Company Act of 2013 has no such exception, and neither does the UK Bribery Act. Nor does the Brazilian law depend on intent: it imposes strict liability on companies, which means a company can be punished for a bribe paid in its interest even if no director knew about it. For that reason, many compliance teams that work in both countries simply prohibit facilitation payments.

In 2025, the US government paused new FCPA investigations for several months and then announced narrower enforcement priorities. Some companies read this as a sign that the authorities would no longer crack down on foreign bribery. Seldom has a reading been so risky. The law itself did not change, conduct that happens today can be investigated years from now, and Brazilian authorities apply their own law whatever Washington decides. Companies that discover a problem and self-report it usually receive more lenient treatment than companies that are caught. So the advice for a company that is crossing the border is simple: write the rules down, train the people, check every intermediary, and when something goes wrong, do not look away.

listenings.text: Every year, somebody in the sales team asks me the same question: can I take this client to dinner? And every year my answer is the same: yes, probably. Hospitality is a normal part of business. But before you book the table, ask yourself three questions. First, who is the guest? If the guest works for a government, or for a company the government owns, you are dealing with a foreign official, and the rules are much stricter. Second, is there a decision pending? Under no circumstances should you invite an official who is deciding on your contract next week. Third, would you be comfortable if the bill appeared in the newspaper tomorrow? If the answer to that one is no, the dinner is too lavish. Only when you can answer all three questions calmly should you pick up the phone and book the restaurant. And please, keep the receipt.

Three years ago, our internal audit found a problem in our new office in Texas. A local agent we had hired to help with permits had received a success fee that was much higher than the market rate, and nobody could explain what services he had actually provided. Never had I been in such a difficult meeting with the board. Some people wanted to deal with it internally and say nothing. I argued that we should investigate properly and self-report. Not only was it the right thing to do, it was also the smart thing to do, because the authorities usually treat companies that come forward better than companies that get caught. We terminated the contract with the agent, we hired outside counsel, and we reported what we had found. The investigation took almost a year. In the end, we paid no fine, but we did change the way we check every intermediary.
